title: GLS Foundations, Part 2: SDC, STA and a GLS-Ready Testbench
description: The timing side of gate-level simulation: SDC as a timing contract, STA basics, reading an STA path report step by step, making your testbench run on the netlist, and how STA and GLS results line up.
content:
In [Part 1](/blog/gls-foundations-part-1-netlists-cells-liberty) we looked at what you're actually simulating in GLS: a netlist built from standard cells, described by Liberty files for timing and Verilog models for behaviour, with delays brought in through the SDF at one PVT corner at a time.

This is Part 2. It covers the timing side: what the design is *supposed* to meet, how STA checks it, how to read the reports STA produces, and how to make sure your testbench is ready to run on the netlist.

---

## 01 — SDC: the timing contract

The SDC file tells synthesis, P&R and STA what the design must meet: the clocks, the I/O timing budgets and the exceptions.

```tcl
create_clock -name core_clk -period 2.0 [get_ports clk_core]     ;# 500 MHz
create_generated_clock -name clk_div2 -source [get_ports clk_core] \
    -divide_by 2 [get_pins u_div/q_reg/Q]
set_clock_uncertainty 0.1 [all_clocks]
set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group core_clk -group apb_clk
set_input_delay  0.6 -clock core_clk [get_ports data_in*]
set_output_delay 0.8 -clock core_clk [get_ports data_out*]

# Valid only if rst_n passes through a reset synchronizer inside the design
set_false_path -from [get_ports rst_n]

# A multicycle path always needs its matching hold adjustment
set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -from [get_cells u_cfg/*_reg*]
set_multicycle_path 1 -hold  -from [get_cells u_cfg/*_reg*]

set_case_analysis 0 [get_ports scan_mode]
```

Two details in that example are easy to get wrong:

- **The false path on reset** is only safe when the reset is synchronized inside the design. If it isn't, removing the path also removes the recovery and removal checks on reset release, which is exactly where reset bugs hide.
- **The multicycle hold line.** With `-setup 2` alone, STA also moves the hold check forward by one cycle. That over-constrains hold and makes P&R insert unnecessary delay buffers. The `-hold 1` line moves the hold check back to the launch edge.

![set_multicycle_path 2 -setup moves the hold check too; -hold 1 moves it back to the launch edge](/blog/gls-p2-02-mcp-hold.png)

A two-cycle path is only valid if the design really behaves that way: the source changes at most every two cycles, and the destination captures only when its enable says so.

```wave
# A two-cycle path: the source changes every 2 cycles, the destination captures every other cycle
clk    : p.......
src    : =.=.=.=. | A B C D
dst_en : 01010101
```

Every line in an SDC is a claim about the design, and many of those claims are DV's to check:

| Construct | What it claims | What DV must check |
|---|---|---|
| create_clock / generated clock | Clock frequencies and dividers | The testbench uses the same periods, and the divider RTL is correct |
| set_clock_groups -asynchronous | Paths between these clocks aren't timed | Every crossing has a synchronizer (CDC signoff) |
| set_input_delay / set_output_delay | Interface timing budget | The testbench drives inputs with realistic delays |
| set_false_path | This path never matters for timing | Prove it, for example that a config register is static while in use |
| set_multicycle_path N | Data has N cycles to arrive | Write an assertion that the enable logic really guarantees N cycles |
| set_case_analysis | Only this mode is analysed | Other modes need their own SDC or runs |

An assertion for the two-cycle multicycle path might look like this:

```systemverilog
// RTL-only check: bind it to the module or wrap it in `ifndef GLS
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  $changed(u_cfg.mode_reg) |=> $stable(u_cfg.mode_reg));
```

It uses an internal signal name, so it belongs in RTL simulation or formal, not in the GLS testbench (more on that in section 04).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> STA trusts the SDC completely. A wrong exception gives you a clean STA report and a silicon failure. Treat every exception as a design claim that DV has to prove.

---

## 02 — STA basics

Static timing analysis checks every timing path without any test vectors. It's exhaustive, but it doesn't understand function, and it relies on the SDC being right. GLS is the opposite: it understands function, but only covers what your tests exercise.

| | STA | Timing GLS |
|---|---|---|
| Vectors | None | Needs tests |
| Coverage | Every path | Only exercised paths |
| Function | Not understood | Understood |
| SDC exceptions | Trusted | Ignored |

Every timing path runs from a **startpoint** (a clock pin or input port) to an **endpoint** (a flop's D pin or an output port). That gives four kinds of path: input to flop, flop to flop, flop to output, and input to output.

The two core checks are:

| Check | Question | Worst corner |
|---|---|---|
| **Setup** | Does new data arrive before the **next** clock edge? | SS |
| **Hold** | Does old data stay stable after the **same** clock edge? | FF |

Slack is how much margin is left. Zero or positive passes. Here are the simplified formulas (they ignore CRPR, which section 03 shows):

```text
Setup slack = (T + T_capture_clk − T_setup − T_uncertainty)
            − (T_launch_clk + T_clk→q + T_logic)

Hold slack  = (T_launch_clk + T_clk→q + T_logic)
            − (T_capture_clk + T_hold + T_uncertainty)
```

The terms you'll see in every report:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Latency | Delay from the clock source to a flop's clock pin |
| Skew | Capture-clock arrival minus launch-clock arrival. Positive skew **helps setup and hurts hold.** |
| Jitter / uncertainty | Clock edge variation plus margin. It shrinks the setup budget and raises the hold requirement. |
| WNS / TNS | Worst negative slack and total negative slack. Max frequency = 1 / (T − WNS). |
| OCV / AOCV / POCV | On-chip variation. STA derates the launch and capture paths in opposite directions. |
| CRPR | Gives back pessimism that was double-counted on the shared part of the clock path |
| MCMM | Signoff over every combination of corner and mode |

STA also runs recovery/removal, minimum pulse width, clock-gating and design-rule checks (max transition, capacitance and fanout), and reports unconstrained paths, which are a coverage hole to review.

When a path fails, the usual fixes are:

- **Setup** (too slow): upsize cells or use faster cells, restructure the logic, pipeline the path, use useful skew, or relax the clock.
- **Hold** (too fast): insert delay buffers, reduce clock skew, or use slower cells.

---

## 03 — How to read an STA path report

Here's a condensed setup report for a 2.0 ns clock at the SS corner:

```text
Startpoint: u_ctrl/state_reg[1] (rising edge-triggered flip-flop clocked by core_clk)
Endpoint:   u_dp/acc_reg[7]      Path Type: max   Corner: ss_100C_1v60

  Delay    Time
   0.00    0.00   clock core_clk (rise edge)            LAUNCH
   0.60    0.60 ^ u_ctrl/state_reg[1]/CLK               launch clock latency
   0.42    1.02 ^ u_ctrl/state_reg[1]/Q                 clk→Q
   1.44    2.46   nand2 / mux2 / a21oi / xor2           logic (mux2 is slowest at 0.46)
   0.02    2.48 ^ u_dp/acc_reg[7]/D                     wire → DATA ARRIVAL

   2.00    2.00   clock core_clk (rise edge)            CAPTURE (next edge)
   0.55    2.55 ^ u_dp/acc_reg[7]/CLK                   capture latency (skew −0.05)
  -0.10    2.45   clock uncertainty
   0.05    2.50   clock reconvergence pessimism (CRPR)
  -0.14    2.36   library setup time → DATA REQUIRED

                 -0.12   slack (VIOLATED)   →  min period 2.12 ns ≈ 471 MHz
```

Read it in two halves. The top half adds up when the data **arrives**: launch clock latency, the flop's clock-to-Q delay, the logic, and the wire. The bottom half works out when the data is **required**: the next clock edge, plus capture latency, minus uncertainty, plus the CRPR credit, minus the flop's setup time. Here the data arrives 0.12 ns too late.

![The same report on a timeline: arrival 2.48 ns, required 2.36 ns, slack −0.12 ns](/blog/gls-p2-01-setup-slack.gif)

A **hold report** has the same layout, but the path type is `min`, the corner is FF, and capture uses the **same** clock edge. Uncertainty and hold time are added to the required time, and slack is arrival minus required.

A good habit is to ask seven questions of every path report:

1. Is it setup or hold, and at which corner?
2. What are the startpoint, endpoint and clocks? Is it the same clock or a crossing?
3. What are the slack and arrival time?
4. How is the time split between clock latency, clock-to-Q, logic and wires?
5. Which cell or wire is slowest, or has the worst slew?
6. Does the skew help or hurt?
7. Is the path real, or should it be an exception? And if it's an exception, who verified it?

If you want to generate these yourself, OpenSTA does it with a few commands:

```tcl
report_checks -path_delay max -fields {slew cap fanout} -digits 3
report_checks -path_delay min
report_checks -from u_ctrl/state_reg[1]/CLK -to u_dp/acc_reg[7]/D
report_wns
report_tns
```

---

## 04 — Getting your testbench ready for GLS

The goal is simple to state: **the exact same test, with the same pass/fail decision, should run on RTL and on the netlist.**

The most common thing that breaks it is hierarchical references like `tb.dut.u_ctrl.state`. After synthesis, modules are flattened, names are escaped (`\u_ctrl/state_reg[0] `), and FSMs may be re-encoded. At best you get compile errors. At worst the test **silently passes while checking nothing**.

![RTL signal names and what synthesis turns them into](/blog/gls-p2-03-rtl-vs-netlist-names.png)

| Technique | How |
|---|---|
| Check at the ports | Scoreboard or reference model on DUT outputs, not internal signals |
| Separate RTL-only code | Wrap internal assertions, coverage and debug in `` `ifndef GLS `` |
| Map paths in one place | Keep `paths_rtl.svh` and `paths_gls.svh` mapping internal names to netlist names |
| Preserve key names | Use dont_touch or keep on a few flops you need to observe (FSM state, status) |
| Use frontdoor register access | Real bus transactions instead of `uvm_hdl_deposit` backdoor writes |
| Avoid races | Drive inputs a little after the clock edge (clocking blocks) and sample before it |
| Handle X on purpose | Use `===` and `!==` in checkers, flag any X on outputs, and decide how non-reset flops are initialized |

> [!TIP]
> Grep your testbench for `dut.`, `force`, `uvm_hdl_` and `bind`. Then compile your RTL with `+define+GLS` and check it still passes. Only then run the netlist.

---

## 05 — How STA and GLS fit together

STA writes the SDF, so timing GLS runs with exactly the delays STA calculated. That makes the two results directly comparable:

| What you see | What it means |
|---|---|
| Setup violation in SS STA | Should appear in SS GLS as a `$setuphold` X or a late capture on the same flop, if a test exercises that path |
| Hold violation in FF STA | Should appear in FF GLS at **any** clock frequency, if a test exercises that path |
| GLS clock sweep | Failures should start once the period drops below T − WNS, provided your tests exercise the worst path |
| GLS violation with no matching STA path | Suspect an SDC exception, testbench timing or SDF annotation, and investigate before waiving |
| Timing GLS looks exactly like zero-delay | The design was compiled with `FUNCTIONAL` or `+nospecify`, or the SDF didn't annotate |

That "if a test exercises it" condition is the core difference between the two. STA sees every path but trusts your constraints. GLS checks real behaviour but only where your tests go. You need both.

When a timing violation does show up in GLS, sort it before you do anything else:

![Triage for a GLS timing violation: is there a matching STA path at this corner?](/blog/gls-p2-04-violation-triage.png)

---

## 06 — Key takeaways, tips and interview questions

### Key takeaways

- **The SDC is a set of claims.** STA trusts every one of them. DV's job is to prove the ones STA can't: false paths, multicycle paths and asynchronous clock groups.
- **Setup is checked on the next edge at the slow corner. Hold is checked on the same edge at the fast corner.** Slowing the clock can't fix a hold failure.
- **Slack is required time minus arrival time.** A path report is just those two sums, line by line.
- **Skew that helps setup hurts hold**, and the other way round.
- **STA sees every path but trusts the constraints. GLS checks real behaviour but only where your tests go.** You need both, and their results should line up.

### Important notes

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **A multicycle path needs both lines.** `-setup N` without `-hold N−1` moves the hold check to the wrong edge and over-constrains it.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **A false path removes every check on that path**, including hold, recovery and removal. Only use it when the path truly can't matter, and write down why.

> [!NOTE]
> **GLS ignores SDC exceptions.** Excepted paths can still produce timing-check violations in GLS. Each one must be classified: expected (waive it with a reason) or a sign that the exception is wrong.

> [!NOTE]
> **A testbench full of hierarchical references isn't GLS-ready**, even if it compiles. It may be checking signals that no longer mean what they did in RTL.

### Practical tips

> [!TIP]
> Before trusting a clean STA report, read the list of exceptions and unconstrained endpoints. A clean report can simply mean things were excluded.

- Ask the **seven questions** of every path report, especially the last one: is this path real, and who verified any exception on it?
- Write an **assertion for every multicycle and false path** the design team declares, and run it in RTL simulation or formal.
- Keep **one file of internal path mappings** for RTL and one for the netlist, instead of scattering hierarchical names through the testbench.
- When GLS shows a violation, **find the matching STA path first**. No match usually means a constraint, testbench or annotation problem.
- Do a **clock sweep** in GLS once: shorten the testbench clock until it fails and compare that period with T − WNS from STA. It builds intuition fast.

### Interview questions

**1. What is an SDC file, and who uses it?**
It's the timing constraint file. Synthesis, place and route, and STA all read it to know the clocks, I/O timing budgets and timing exceptions.

**2. Why is the SDC relevant to a DV engineer?**
Its exceptions are claims about design behaviour that STA trusts without checking. DV proves them with assertions, CDC checks and timing GLS.

**3. What's the difference between setup and hold checks?**
Setup checks that new data arrives before the next capturing edge. Hold checks that old data stays stable long enough after the same edge it was launched on.

**4. Why do you need `-hold` when you set a multicycle path with `-setup 2`?**
`-setup 2` moves the hold check forward by one cycle as well. Without `set_multicycle_path 1 -hold`, hold is checked against the wrong edge and becomes over-constrained.

**5. What are the risks of `set_false_path` on an asynchronous reset?**
It removes recovery and removal checks on reset release. That's only safe if the reset is synchronized inside the design.

**6. Why is `set_false_path` a poor choice for multi-bit clock domain crossings?**
It leaves the crossing with no delay limit, so skew between bits is unbounded. `set_max_delay -datapath_only` bounds the delay while still ignoring the clock relationship.

**7. What do positive and negative skew do to setup and hold?**
Positive skew (capture clock later) gives setup more time and makes hold harder. Negative skew does the opposite.

**8. What is CRPR?**
Clock reconvergence pessimism removal. The shared part of the launch and capture clock paths can't be both fast and slow at once, so STA gives back that double-counted pessimism.

**9. A path has −0.12 ns setup slack at a 2.0 ns clock. What's its maximum frequency?**
1 / (2.0 + 0.12) ns ≈ 471 MHz.

**10. What are WNS and TNS?**
Worst negative slack is the single worst path. Total negative slack is the sum of all negative slacks, which shows how widespread the problem is.

**11. Why might your RTL testbench pass on the netlist but check nothing?**
Hierarchical references may point at signals that were renamed, re-encoded or optimized away, so checks silently compare the wrong thing or nothing at all.

**12. GLS shows a setup violation, but STA is clean at that corner. What do you check?**
Whether the path is covered by an SDC exception, whether the testbench drives inputs too close to the clock edge, and whether the SDF annotated correctly for that netlist and corner.

**13. Why can STA and GLS disagree, and which one is right?**
STA covers every path but relies on the constraints. GLS covers only exercised paths but uses real behaviour. A disagreement means one tool's assumption is wrong, and that has to be found, not waived.

**14. How would you choose which tests to run in timing GLS?**
Focus on what timing-sensitive behaviour depends on: reset and boot, clock and power-mode changes, high-activity datapath tests, DFT patterns and any ECO-affected logic, at the SS and FF corners.

---

That completes the foundations. The next step is to run it: take a small FIFO from RTL to a sky130 netlist with Yosys, run the same testbench on both, and plant a few bugs that pass RTL but fail GLS. That's where these concepts start to stick.

### Further reading

- Don Mills and Clifford Cummings, *RTL Coding Styles That Yield Simulation and Synthesis Mismatches* (SNUG 1999).
- Mike Turpin, *The Dangers of Living with an X* (SNUG 2003).
- Clifford Cummings' papers on resets and clock domain crossing, at sunburst-design.com/papers.
- J. Bhasker and Rakesh Chadha, *Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs*.
- OpenSTA documentation, for running the report commands yourself.
